founded.what: The year the founding charter of the house was drawn up at Reims, on 1 September, by the house's own account.

kind.means: A négociant manipulant, a house in the trade's own word: it buys grapes from growers in forty or fifty crus beyond its own vines and makes the wine itself in Reims.

story: Ruinart traces its idea to Dom Thierry Ruinart (1657 to 1709), a Benedictine monk and scholar who died at the abbey of Hautvillers. His nephew drew up the founding charter of the house at Reims on 1 September 1729, by the house's account, and the house calls itself the first established Champagne house. It also says that in 1764 it shipped a rosé Champagne across Europe. Its wines came to age in the Gallo-Roman chalk pits beneath Reims, listed as a historic monument in 1931. The family led the house until 1963, when it passed to Moët & Chandon, and with Moët Hennessy it joined LVMH in 1987. The first vintage of Dom Ruinart, a Blanc de Blancs named for the monk, was the 1959, launched in 1966, and the first Dom Ruinart Rosé followed with the 1966 vintage. On 4 July 2015 UNESCO listed the Champagne hillsides, houses and cellars as World Heritage, the chalk pits of the Saint-Nicaise hill among them. With the 2010 vintage Dom Ruinart went back to ageing under natural cork in place of a metal cap, and the 2013 was the second so aged.

style.line: Chardonnay leads the whole range, even where Pinot Noir is in the blend: delicate, fresh and precise, with the chalk cellars of Reims giving a long, quiet ageing.
style.grapes: Chardonnay above all, from the Côte des Blancs and the Montagne de Reims; R de Ruinart adds Pinot Noir and a little Meunier, from 40 to 50 crus, by the house.
style.reserve: 20 to 30 per cent reserve wines from several years in both Blanc de Blancs and R de Ruinart, by the house.
style.lees: At least nine years for Dom Ruinart 2010, by the house, the whole cuvée taking about twelve years to make.
style.dosage: 7 grams a litre for Blanc de Blancs and R de Ruinart, 4 for Dom Ruinart 2010, by the house.

nv.name: Ruinart Blanc de Blancs
nv.note: The non vintage most guests know, in its clear, rounded bottle: Chardonnay alone from 25 to 30 crus, with 20 to 30 per cent reserve wines, by the house.

cuvee.name: Dom Ruinart Blanc de Blancs

first.what: The first vintage, launched in 1966, by the house.

cuvee.rhythm: Made only in years the house declares since the 1959: one of its pages counts twenty seven vintages, and the 2009, 2010 and 2013 are among those it has shown.
cuvee.blend: Chardonnay alone, from the Côte des Blancs and the Montagne de Reims, the Côte des Blancs always the larger part.
cuvee.sites: For the 2010, by the house: Grand Cru Chardonnay, nine tenths from Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, Avize, Chouilly and Cramant on the Côte des Blancs, one tenth from Sillery on the Montagne de Reims. The 2013 drew seven tenths from the Côte des Blancs, with Premier Cru villages too.
cuvee.making: A vintage Blanc de Blancs blended from Grand Cru villages of both slopes. From the 2010 the bottles age under natural cork rather than a metal crown cap, which the house says keeps the wine fresh and lends notes of grilled almond and coffee over the years. Every bottle is disgorged by hand, and the 2010 was dosed at 4 grams a litre.
cuvee.lees: At least nine years on its lees for the 2010, by the house.
cuvee.young: Fig leaf, black tea and fresh spices by the house's note on the first vintage aged under cork, with white pepper and roasted espresso over a silky mousse, and a long, fresh finish with a fine bitterness.
cuvee.aged: Aged under cork, it gathers grilled almond and coffee after some ten years, in the house's words, the chalky freshness staying beneath.

forms.name: Dom Ruinart Rosé
forms.note: The vintage rosé of the same name, first made with the 1966 vintage: Chardonnay coloured with a little red wine of Pinot Noir.

cuvee.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius, never ice cold; no need to decant; a tulip or a white wine glass.

table.house45: Ruinart is the house of Reims that calls itself the first established Champagne house, with a founding charter of 1729. It takes its spirit from Dom Thierry Ruinart, a Benedictine monk and the founder's uncle. Its wines rest in Gallo-Roman chalk pits deep beneath the city, part of the UNESCO listing of 2015. The style is led by Chardonnay right across the range, fresh and precise. Most guests know the Blanc de Blancs in its clear, rounded bottle. The prestige cuvée is Dom Ruinart, a vintage Blanc de Blancs first made in 1959.
table.house10: Ruinart is the Reims house of 1729 that calls itself the first established Champagne house, Chardonnay led and aged in Roman chalk pits.
table.cuvee45: Dom Ruinart is the prestige Champagne of Ruinart, a vintage Blanc de Blancs named for the monk who inspired the house. It is Chardonnay alone, most of it from Grand Cru villages of the Côte des Blancs, with a little from the Montagne de Reims. Its first vintage was 1959. From the 2010 the house went back to ageing it under natural cork rather than a metal cap. Expect fig leaf, white pepper and roasted coffee over a silky, fine bubble. I serve it cool but never ice cold, in a white wine glass.
table.sale: If you love Chardonnay, Dom Ruinart is the vintage Blanc de Blancs of a house that dates itself from 1729, aged for years in its Roman chalk pits. Shall I bring a bottle for the table?
table.cuvee10: Dom Ruinart is the vintage Blanc de Blancs of Ruinart, Grand Cru Chardonnay first made in 1959.
table.cuvee20: Dom Ruinart is Ruinart's vintage Blanc de Blancs, Chardonnay from the Côte des Blancs and the Montagne de Reims. Since the 2010 it has aged under natural cork, with fig leaf, white pepper and roasted coffee.

guests.q: Is Dom Ruinart the same as Dom Pérignon?
guests.a: No. Dom Ruinart is the Chardonnay prestige cuvée of Ruinart, of Reims, named for the monk Dom Thierry Ruinart; Dom Pérignon is Moët & Chandon's, named for another monk, and is a blend of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

guests.q: Is Ruinart really the oldest Champagne house?
guests.a: It calls itself the first established Champagne house, from 1729. Gosset dates itself earlier, from 1584, but as a house of still wine, which is why both claims stand.
The family led it until 1963, when it passed to Moët & Chandon, and it joined LVMH with Moët Hennessy in 1987.
Dom is the title of a Benedictine monk. Dom Thierry Ruinart was the founder's uncle, and the house says his ideas inspired its founding.

traps: Ruinart is the oldest Champagne house (1729); Gosset is the oldest wine house in Champagne (1584) but began with still wine.
Dom Ruinart is Ruinart's prestige cuvée, a Blanc de Blancs; Dom Pérignon is Moët & Chandon's, a blend of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
Dom Thierry Ruinart was the founder's uncle, a monk who died in 1709: he did not found the house.
Dom Ruinart is a Blanc de Blancs, but Dom Ruinart Rosé is Chardonnay coloured with red Pinot Noir: the same name on a different wine.

questions.q: A guest wants the vintage Blanc de Blancs named for a Benedictine monk, from the house founded at Reims in 1729. Which cuvée is it?
questions.exp: Dom Ruinart is Ruinart's Chardonnay prestige cuvée, named for Dom Thierry Ruinart. Dom Pérignon, named for another monk, is Moët & Chandon's blend; Comtes de Champagne is Taittinger's Blanc de Blancs and Le Mesnil is Salon's.

questions.q: Which claim does Ruinart make of itself, and Gosset not?
opts: The first established Champagne house, from 1729
The oldest wine house of Champagne, from 1584
The first known blended rosé, of 1818
questions.exp: Ruinart calls itself the first established Champagne house, from 1729. Gosset dates itself as a house of still wine from 1584, and the blended rosé and the riddling table are credited to Veuve Clicquot.

questions.q: What changed in the making of Dom Ruinart from the 2010 vintage?
opts: The bottles aged under natural cork
It became a blend of several vintages
The wine fermented in new oak
questions.exp: From the 2010 the house returned to ageing Dom Ruinart under natural cork in place of a metal cap. It remains Chardonnay alone and a vintage wine; Pinot Noir colours only the rosé.

report: Built on the library's p-ruinart, contradicting it nowhere; its trap on the oldest Champagne house against the oldest wine house is kept word for word, and Gosset's record carries the same pair.

For the owner: the library names the non vintage Brut Ruinart Brut, formerly R de Ruinart, while the house's British page and its 2015 vintage still carry R de Ruinart; this record uses R de Ruinart and does not edit the library.

Dom Thierry Ruinart's dates, 1657 to 1709, are the house's; a second account confirms his death in 1709 at Hautvillers. The nephew who founded the house is described, not named: his dates were not found.
The founding charter of 1 September 1729 and the rosé shipped in 1764 rest on the house's pages alone and are told as its account.

The chalk pits: one account dates their purchase to 1768 and another to 1877, so the record does not date it; the listing as a historic monument in 1931 is one secondary account and the refuter should confirm it.
The sale of 1963 to Moët & Chandon rests on VinePair, Millesima and the French culture ministry's inventory as a search summary gave them; one account gives a share of 80 per cent, left out.
kind.code: the letters NM were not read on a label; they are inferred from the house buying from 40 to 50 crus.
Style fields: vessels and malolactic are empty, no page read stating them.

Dom Ruinart's sites change by vintage: Grand Cru only and nine tenths Côte des Blancs for the 2010, Grand and Premier Cru and seven tenths for the 2013, by the house; the blend line says only that the Côte des Blancs is the larger part.
The vintage count of twenty seven is one house page's, undated; other accounts give twenty one and twenty four at other dates.

Dom Ruinart Rosé's first vintage, 1966, rests on Decanter's report of the house's fiftieth anniversary tasting; its colouring by red Pinot Noir is the general account and the refuter should read a house sheet.
